transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-08-29
Start time (UTC): 15:30
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Marcus (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Liam O'Connor (CTO, Sentra), Nisha Patel (ML Lead), Hector Alvarez (Platform)

Summary:
Sentra Logix is evaluating Redwood for a hybrid deployment — Hosted for non-sensitive workloads, Dedicated for prediction at scale, and Private/VPC for regulated customer data paths. Main evaluation axes: open model compatibility (quantized vs fp16), long-context support (they want 80k+ tokens for legal doc summarization), multilingual coverage (English + Swahili + Spanish), tool-calling (internal search + DB lookup + external verified calculators). They asked about KMS integration, audit logs, and canary rollouts. Next steps: pilot setup, security docs, sample data for benchmarks.

Topics covered:
- Model families and tokenizer caveats (LLaMA2, Mistral, Mosaic, Luminous approximations)
- Context length tradeoffs (KV cache, segmenting, sparse attention)
- Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private (latency, cost, data residency)
- Tool-calling patterns and function-calling support (schema, retries, auth)
- Security: KMS/HSM, SSO, SAML, audit logs, SOC2

Action items (as recorded): see metadata for details

Transcript body:
[00:00] Marcus: alright hello everyone, thanks for making time. I'm Marcus from Redwood, AE on this region.
[00:08] Liam: Hey Marcus, hey Priya, Liam here. We want to get into the nitty gritty — particularly model compat and how long context works with your runtime.
[00:15] Priya: hi! great to be here. quick agenda: model compatibility, context length and KV cache behavior, multilingual and tokenization issues, then tool-calling and deployment modes. we'll leave time for questions.
[00:28] Nisha: sounds good. quick background: Sentra's product ingests contracts and generates executive summaries, Q&A, and redline suggestions. Some documents are 50–100 pages. We also have Spanish and East African languages in scope — low resource like Swahili. We want to avoid hallucinations on legal citations.
[00:48] Hector: on infra side, we run a hybrid cloud — core services in GCP, some customer-hosted clusters in Azure. For regulated customers we must avoid sending raw PII offsite. so VPC or on-prem is required there.
[01:02] Marcus: great, so first is model families. we support a catalog of open models — community LLaMA2 variants, Mistral variants, some Mosaic weights, and a few high-context families. important thing: some models have different tokenizer behavior which affects effective context length.
[01:18] Nisha: can you expand on tokenizer behavior? we ran into weird truncation once where a newline got tokenized into many tokens and blew our budget.
[01:26] Priya: yeah that happens — newlines and certain unicode can spike token counts. our runtime exposes tokenization stats per request so you can monitor token inflation. for long context we do two levers: 1) KV cache streaming where prior turns are kept in GPU KV cache to avoid re-encoding; 2) prefix sharding — we can keep embeddings + chunk index and only include most relevant chunks to the decoder. both reduce cost but have tradeoffs for strict linear context semantics.
[01:55] Liam: you mentioned KV cache — is that persisted across requests or only per session? if they go stale what happens?
[02:03] Priya: good q. KV cache is session-local in the default hosted runtime; it persists for the lifetime of the conversation instance. for Dedicated and Private we can optionally persist checkpointed caches to disk (encrypted) to rehydrate for long-running flows. if caches become stale due to model updates we do automatic invalidation and can fall back to re-encoding. sometimes it's transcribed as K-V cash in logs, lol.
[02:30] Nisha: about the 80k token ask — is that realistic? we need 80k full tokens for entire contracts occasionally.
[02:37] Marcus: depends on model family. some of the newer 'long-context' variants support 100k+ by using block-sparse attention or efficient linear attention. we also recommend chunked retrieval+rerank so you don't feed 100k tokens to the decoder every time. but for extractive summarization we can stage the pipeline: retrieval -> compressed representations -> decoder.
[02:58] Hector: latency implications? if we stitch 80k chunks into a single pass it's going to be slow.
[03:04] Priya: yes, single-pass large contexts add latency and memory. our Dedicated pools allow predictable throughput and we can tune batch sizes and quantization to reduce GPU memory. for example, running a 70–100k pass on a 80GB A100 will require model sharding or a 2x GPU configuration. we usually recommend a hybrid approach: Dedicated for heavy offline/full-doc ops, Hosted for low-latency user interactions.
[03:28] Liam: on cost model — do you price by token or by reserved capacity?
[03:33] Marcus: Hosted is usage-based per token. Dedicated is reserved capacity plus a lower per-token unit for the model service. Private is licensed plus infra costs. We'll send the detailed pricing sheet.
[03:42] Nisha: model quantization — will quantized weights change outputs enough for legal summarization? precision matters.
[03:50] Priya: quantization affects some exactness. We offer quantization profiles: 4-bit W8-like for throughput but sometimes reduces determinism on numeric outputs. For legal citations we recommend fp16 or bfloat16 if you need numeric fidelity. For the pilot we can test both and track rouge/qa metrics.
[04:09] [Speaker 1: 04:09] Nisha: (mumbled) some of our team tried q4_k_m and saw missing parentheses in citations.
[04:16] Priya: yup that's a common artifact. our Optimize toolkit will recommend quant profiles given your prompt set.
[04:22] Hector: about tool-calling — we have internal search, a Postgres DB, and a signed-document verifier service. How would Redwood handle function calls and auth to our internal services?
[04:34] Marcus: we support structured function calling and recommend you use Signed requests via a short-lived service token. In Private or Dedicated you can configure a private VPC route so the runtime calls back into your services over peered network. For Hosted we provide a callback with JWT exchange through our relay.
[04:51] Nisha: any guards for tool-calling to avoid exfiltration — like allowlist of endpoints and payload redaction?
[04:57] Priya: yes, we do per-route allowlists, schema validation, and you can enforce an outbound policy. we also log function inputs/outputs to audit logs — these logs can be stored in your KMS-backed bucket for compliance, or disabled for certain routes.
[05:14] Liam: on security: SOC2 plus SSO — how hard is SAML integration and RBAC for multiple teams?
[05:21] Marcus: SAML/SSO is standard, we also support SCIM provisioning. RBAC is role-based at the org, project, and token level. Audit logs are immutable and we support log export into your SIEM. we'll attach our security pack with diagrams.
[05:36] Hector: we also need to ensure crypto — we use Google KMS but want HSM for some customers.
[05:42] Priya: Private deployments can integrate with customer KMS/HSM. For Hosted we integrate with cloud KMS providers and can offer bring-your-own-key for encryption-at-rest.
[05:51] [00:05:52] Marcus: switching back to models — have you run any in-house evals? what quality metrics do you track?
[05:58] Nisha: we track citation accuracy, F1 for extraction, rouge for summaries, and a custom legality check that flags hallucinated statute numbers. Our baseline is a tuned Llama2-70B variant.
[06:10] Priya: ok cool. for comparisons we can run a small A/B on Llama2-70B-quantized vs a Mistral-long-extended and a Mosaic variant. we'll instrument token-level latency and per-response confidence signals.
[06:23] Liam: will Redwood support running our eval harness? we have a pytest-based runner.
[06:27] Marcus: yes — we can run your harness inside a Controlled Dedicated pilot (we'll need dockerized runner or a reproducible script).
[06:35] Nisha: multilingual — particularly Swahili. LLMs often underperform on low-resource languages. any support there?
[06:41] Priya: we have model profiles that include multilingual benchmarks. For Swahili, sometimes translation+monolingual LLM pipeline performs better: translate to English, generate, then translate back, plus a Swahili-tuned adapter if you need native tokens. We can also provision a small adapter fine-tune on your labeled data.
[06:58] Hector: fine-tuning in Dedicated/Private — can we run continuous fine-tunes or adapters?
[07:04] Marcus: yes, we support parameter-efficient fine-tuning workflows and adapters. In Private you can host training loops; in Dedicated we can run finetunes in an isolated subpool. Note: any fine-tuned weights you generate can be pinned to rollout policies.
[07:19] Nisha: rollouts — we want canary 10% then ramp with automatic rollback based on QA regression.
[07:25] Priya: Redwood Console supports rollout policies, automatic rollback when metrics drift beyond thresholds, and A/B. For Dedicated we can map traffic to GPU pools.
[07:35] [00:07:36] Liam: about observability — we need token-level cost breakouts per route and per-customer.
[07:42] Marcus: yep. Console has token-cost heatmaps, per-request traces, and you can tag requests with customer_id so cost is broken down.
[07:50] Nisha: question: for private deployment on our infra, is there any Redwood control plane talking to your cloud? we need to be air-gapped for some accounts.
[07:58] Priya: we have two Private modes: connected control plane with peered management endpoints, and fully air-gapped on-prem install — the latter uses a one-time license/key and all telemetry stays local. For air-gapped we ship an appliance package.
[08:15] Hector: if we go Dedicated managed, what's the SLA and snapshot policy?
[08:20] Marcus: our Dedicated tiers have multi-availability pools and an SLA on latency/uptime; snapshot policies are configurable — we do encrypted checkpointing. We'll share the SLA PDF.
[08:28] Nisha: any pitfalls we should be aware of when comparing Anthropic or OpenAI hosted endpoints vs Redwood?
[08:35] Priya: the main differences are serving semantics and control. OpenAI/Anthropic are great for simplicity, but if you need predictable latency at scale, private KMS, VPC peering, or model pinning for audits, using a platform like Redwood gives more ops control. There's also cost levers — batching, quantization, and caching — that reduce per-token bill with little change to API.
[08:58] Liam: what about model provenance and versioning? we need a way to prove which model version generated a particular answer for compliance.
[09:05] Marcus: we include model version identifiers in request metadata and immutable traces in the audit log. You can pin model versions to routes and get a hash of the model weights for attestation.
[09:18] Nisha: can we run a stress test — 150 concurrent users hitting long summarization?
[09:23] Priya: yes, for Dedicated we can provision a temporary burst pool. For hosted we can set rate-limits; we'd recommend the Dedicated pilot for that scale.
[09:33] Hector: networking — do you support VPC peering vs PrivateLink vs VPN?
[09:39] Marcus: we support VPC peering and private connections. For Azure we support VNet peering. For very strict cases we recommend Private deployment.
[09:48] [00:09:49] Nisha: about data retention — logs, transcripts — can we TTL logs after 30 days?
[09:55] Priya: configurable retention policies per dataset/route, yes. For compliance we can export and then delete from Redwood after ingest.
[10:03] Liam: can Redwood's runtime do model-switch routing? for example, cheap model for drafting, high-accuracy pinned model for finalization.
[10:11] Marcus: yes, smart routing supports policy-based routing — by latency, cost, or fallback. You can route by route name or per-customer. We'll show a routing example in the pilot runbook.
[10:21] Nisha: prompt engineering — occasionally tool-calling requires strict schema. do you support function signatures and automatic validation?
[10:28] Priya: yes — function calling with JSON schema validation, retries, backoff, and per-call auth headers. We also provide a simulator for testing tool-calls offline.
[10:37] Hector: last infrastructure q: will we get container-level metrics? GPU utilization?
[10:42] Marcus: console exposes per-instance GPU metrics, token throughput, queue depths; for Dedicated we can also push metrics to your Prometheus endpoint.
[10:51] [00:10:52] Liam: ok looks good. what do we need to kick off the pilot?
[10:56] Marcus: we'll need: 1) three prompt templates and sample doc set, 2) an agreed metric rubric (Nisha's team), 3) infra diagram for VPC/peering (Hector). Priya will run the perf tests.
[11:09] Nisha: timeline — we want a pilot next week ideally.
[11:13] Priya: Priya: i can start the runbook this week; propose start date 2026-09-06.
[11:18] Marcus: i'll send the pricing and legal contact. we'll also attach the SOC2 package.
[11:23] Hector: we'll get the infra docs by 2026-09-03.
[11:26] [00:11:27] Nisha: quick note — please include tokenization examples for the models you plan to test so we can sanity-check truncation.
[11:33] Priya: will do — we'll include a tokenization sample and an adapter plan for Swahili.
[11:38] Liam: thanks all, that's useful.
[11:40] Marcus: thanks everyone. we'll recap in email. any final Qs?
[11:46] Nisha: none for now.
[11:48] Marcus: great, talk soon.

End of meeting
